item.title: Nvidia, AI Industry Face Prospect of Future Without Huang
item.description:
Bloomberg's Emily Chang said that while Nvidia will survive the ouster of CEO Jensen Huang, questions remain about if it will be able to thrive in the same way without Huang's relationships with global leaders and no predetermined successor. Chang said the national security implications around the company are in the spotlight going forward, as Colette Kress, the interim CEO in the wake of Huang's resignation, also believes that Nvidia should be able to sell the most advanced chips to China. item.title: 'Essential' That US Upholds Export Controls on Chips, Says Ben Buchanan
item.description:
Ben Buchanan, former White House special advisor for Artificial Intelligence in the Biden Administration and author of the new book 'The Bitter Struggle: Superintelligence, Superpowers, and the Fate of the World,' said that it is 'essential' that the US maintain its curbs around exports of US chips to China and is 'more urgent now' given the lead the US has in the AI race. Buchanan said that the Trump administration made a mistake in not enforcing the Biden administration's 'diffusion rule,' which extended strict controls on AI chip exports to stop chips from reaching adversaries. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The Perfect Storm That Clobbered Hedge Funds
item.description:
Even before the midterms, the AI trade was weakening. Just look at all the headlines from October in the hedge fund world — it was one of the bloodiest periods the industry has faced in recent memory. Now, after the blue wave, things continue to look uncertain. So what's going to happen with the AI buildout now? And what about the big Anthropic IPO? Today's episode is a two-parter, one that examines both the hedge fund carnage of the last few weeks and the broader macro conditions we find ourselves in after the midterm elections. We speak with two of our Bloomberg News colleagues — Nishant Kumar, chief correspondent for hedge funds, and macro strategist Michael Ball — and they help lay out why October was a historic month for hedge funds and what they are paying attention to now as jitters from the AI trade continue to work their way through the market. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
According to Joshua Goodman, trash collection in New York is one of the last services the city offers that is not yet touched by neoliberalism. What he means is that it's the last free and unlimited city service — there is no opt-in; it is not means tested. Goodman — who is the DSNY's deputy commissioner for public affairs and customer experience — tells us that the city deals with 24 million pounds of trash every day, and on today's podcast, he explains the logistical dance required to sort through all that garbage. We also get into why NYC produces less trash than you might think, the DSNY's new containerization program (and the new side-loading trucks they built in less than 18 months), and why recycling is not a scam. Get a jump start on the US trading day with Dani Burger on "Bloomberg Open Interest." A blowout jobs report fuels expectations for another Fed rate hike, even as Wall Street reels from a nearly $4 trillion tech selloff and mounting questions about the AI trade. Plus, Anthropic's IPO prospects and valuation reset, BlackRock CIO Rick Rieder explains the AI unwind and emerging credit opportunities, Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council, discusses inflation and Fed policy, and Greg Ebel, CEO of Enbridge Energy, weighs in on the growing energy demands of AI infrastructure. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Kok Leong Chan

item.title: The Macro Implications of the Blue Tsunami
item.description:
We don't need to tell you that the midterm elections were historic: The Democrats won bigger than even they imagined. But as the dust settles, an open question we are puzzling over is the market's ongoing reaction to this massive political sea change. Democratic control of Congress — and control over a number of formerly red statehouses like Texas and Iowa — will influence everything from the composition of the FOMC to data center construction. And what we're seeing right now, with stocks like Tesla and SpaceX tumbling, is a direct response to these conditions. To get a better sense of this macro moment, we turn to Odd Lots regular, Employ America's executive director Skanda Amarnath to talk about how the midterms will influence the Fed's battle with inflation, Elon Musk's political instincts, and what a Democratic majority means for the market, tariffs, and AI. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Omar El Chmouri and Laura Gardner Cuesta

item.title: An Election Day Special With Nate Silver
item.description:
Nate Silver tells us he is calling this midterms the “rock and a hard place election” — the background conditions are great for Democrats to win both the House and the Senate, but for that to come to pass, the party has to pull off some things that haven't happened in generations, like winning Texas. To believe that will happen requires a certain leap of faith, which is anathema to pollsters. Still, the polls generally believe Democrats are favored, but many professional pollsters would end up with egg on their face if the night does not go that way. Silver — the founder of Silver Bulletin — joins us today to discuss why popular narratives around polling error are wrong, prediction markets, why he doesn't think AI will replace pollsters, and what he is paying attention to tonight as the polls close. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: The $300 Billion Structured Notes Market Is Booming
item.description:
The structured products business in the US has gotten very large recently — on track to hit $300 billion in sales this year. What was once an opaque financial product is getting a lot more attention. So what are structured products, exactly, and how are they influencing the economy? In short, structured products are basically a fusion of a bank IOU with a derivative product, but that underplays how complex they are and how they are shaping market dynamics. On this episode, we speak with Alex Micalizzi, who is the international head of equity structured notes at Nomura, and he gives us what might be the clearest explanation of how structured products are created, how they work, and why sales in structured products has grown so much in the last year. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Hilton Dips, JetBlue Rallies | Stock Movers
item.description:
Today's biggest winners and losers in the stock market. On this episode of Stock Movers: - Hilton Worldwide (HLT) is falling after the hotel operator gave a forecast for adjusted earnings per share for the fourth quarter that fell short of the average analyst estimate. - JetBlue (JBLU) shares are rallying after the carrier reiterated its expectation to deliver at least $1 in earnings per share and positive free cash flow in 2028. The shares closed Monday at a record low as the airline grapples with cash burn and elevated oil prices. - Boeing (BA) shares are on the move after posted a quarterly loss after higher costs affected its commercial-jet business. The company's total revenue grew about 4% to $24.19 billion, driven in part by stronger sales from its defense, space and security business. Boeing generated cash despite the loss, and its 737 program is progressing toward stabilized production at 47 jets a month. (Source: Bloomberg)

European stocks hit a session high as a decline in oil prices and robust US economic data more than offset disappointing earnings from benchmark heavyweight HSBC Holdings Plc.

item.title: US Plans Two-Month Extension to Shipping-Fee Truce With China
item.description:
The US may extend a pause on charges for Chinese-linked ships for calling at American ports by two months, following efforts to iron out broader trade issues between the two economies.
